provocative

pruh-VOK-uh-tiv -- built on the root '-voc-,' meaning to call. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Provocative is intended or likely to cause an argument or heated discussion, often deliberately.

The columnist's provocative essay was clearly designed to spark outrage and debate.

Example

A stand-up comedian opens her new special with a deliberately provocative joke about a controversial news story, fully expecting half the audience to laugh and the other half to boo.

That deliberate stirring up of strong opinions and reactions is what makes the joke provocative. Unlike 'offensive,' which is usually unintentional or purely negative, provocative implies the reaction was the whole point.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

incendiary: Incendiary language is meant to set feelings ablaze -- it stirs conflict the way a match starts a fire, and it often borders on dangerous. Provocative is broader and cooler: a provocative essay wants strong reactions and debate, not necessarily rage.

edgy: Edgy describes a style that flirts with the limits of what is acceptable -- daring and a little uncomfortable, but not aimed at any one target. Provocative goes further: it is intended to cause an argument or heated discussion, and the reaction is the whole point.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

soothing: having a calming or relaxing effect

inoffensive: not likely to upset or offend anyone

Where it sits · how much anger it aims to stir — controversial → provocative → inflammatory

controversial vs. provocative: Controversial is milder than provocative in some uses -- something controversial simply causes disagreement, while provocative implies the reaction was deliberately intended, and often more emotionally charged.

inflammatory vs. provocative: Inflammatory can feel even more intense than provocative: provocative aims to provoke a reaction, but inflammatory specifically implies stirring up anger or hostility, almost like lighting a fire.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — pro-

prefix — pro-: forth (Latin)

root — -voc-

root — -voc-: to call (Latin (vocare))

suffix — -ative

suffix — -ative: tending to (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin vocare meant 'to call,' pro- means 'forth,' and -ative marks 'tending to' -- so provocative describes something tending to call forth a reaction, whether anger, debate, or laughter.
